reference_text:
Welcome to the course. We will work through each concept carefully, connect the
ideas step by step, and use practical examples to make technical topics easier
to understand. When we introduce a new method, focus first on the problem it
solves and why it is useful. For example, in machine learning, features are the
information we give the model, while the target is what we want it to predict.
Now consider a simple question: what changes when the data contains missing
values? We will think through the reason and then look at the code. In Python,
we can inspect the data, run one small step at a time, and explain what the
result means. The goal is to understand the logic, not simply memorize syntax.

slides.title: Advanced Python Techniques
slides.transcript:
Welcome to Module 7, Advanced Python Techniques.

Up to this point, we have spent a lot of time building a strong foundation in Python. We have worked with variables, conditions, loops, functions, data structures, and ways to organize our code.

In this module, we are going to take some of those ideas and look at more compact and more powerful ways to write Python.

You will see techniques such as list comprehensions, lambda functions, and generators. We will also spend some time on debugging and code efficiency.

I want to emphasize something from the beginning. Advanced Python does not necessarily mean writing the shortest code possible. Short code can sometimes become difficult to understand.

Our goal is to write code that is clear, useful, and appropriate for the problem we are solving.

These techniques are especially helpful in analytics because we often need to filter values, transform data, sort records, or process large collections.

As we move through the examples, try to focus less on memorizing the syntax and more on understanding what each technique is helping us accomplish.

slides.title: Learning path for Module 7
slides.transcript:
Here is our learning path for this module.

We are going to work through five main ideas.

The first topic is list comprehensions. A list comprehension gives us a compact way to create a new list from an existing collection of values.

Next, we will look at lambda functions. A lambda is basically a very small function that we can define in one expression. You will often see lambda functions used with operations such as sorting.

After that, we will study generators. Generators are useful when we want Python to produce values one at a time instead of creating everything in memory at once.

Then we will discuss debugging. Even experienced programmers spend a lot of time debugging. So we will look at simple techniques for understanding what is happening inside our code.

Finally, we will discuss efficiency and built-in Python functions.

By the end of this module, you should be able to recognize these patterns, explain what they are doing, and decide when using them actually makes your code better.

You do not need to force these techniques into every program. The important skill is knowing when they are useful.

slides.title: List Comprehensions
slides.transcript:
Let's begin with list comprehensions.

A list comprehension is a shorter way to create a new list using a loop.

Look at the first example.

We have x squared for x in range five.

If this syntax feels strange at first, think about the regular loop that would do the same thing.

We would create an empty list, loop through the numbers from zero through four, calculate x squared, and then append each result to the list.

The list comprehension combines those steps into one line.

Before you run the first cell, try to predict the result.

We start with zero, then one, two, three, and four. Each number is squared. So we should get zero, one, four, nine, and sixteen.

Go ahead and run the cell and confirm the result.

The second example adds a condition.

We have a list of ages, and we only want values greater than or equal to eighteen.

You can read the comprehension almost like a sentence: give me each age from the ages list if that age is at least eighteen.

Run the example and look at which values remain.

Then try changing one of the ages. For example, change seventeen to eighteen and run the cell again.

This is a very common analytical pattern: start with a collection, apply a rule, and create a new collection from the values that meet that rule.

slides.title: Lambda Functions
slides.transcript:
Now let's look at lambda functions.

A lambda is a small anonymous function.

Anonymous simply means that we can create the function without giving it a normal function name using def.

Look at the first example.

We write lambda x: x times two.

The x represents the input, and everything after the colon is the expression that produces the result.

So if we pass five into this lambda, Python returns ten.

For a simple example like this, we could absolutely write a regular function instead.

The advantage of lambda becomes more obvious when we need a small function temporarily.

Look at the second example.

We have sales data stored as tuples. Each tuple contains a label and a sales value.

We want to sort the records based on the sales value.

The key parameter tells sorted what part of each item it should examine.

Our lambda receives one item and returns item at index one, which is the numeric sales value.

We also use reverse equals true because we want the largest value first.

Run this example and notice the order of A, B, and C.

A useful rule is this: if your lambda becomes complicated or difficult to explain, it is probably better to create a regular named function instead.

slides.title: Generators & yield
slides.transcript:
Now we are moving to generators.

Generators are important because they allow Python to produce values one at a time.

Let's compare that with a regular list.

If we create a list containing one million transformed values, Python normally creates and stores all one million values in memory.

A generator can work differently. It can calculate a value when we need it, return that value, and then continue later.

The key word that makes this possible is yield.

Look at the squares_gen function.

We loop through the numbers up to n.

Instead of using return, we use yield.

When Python reaches yield, it gives us one value and pauses the function.

The next time Python asks the generator for another value, the function continues from where it stopped.

Run the example.

You will see the squared values printed one at a time.

For four values, memory is obviously not a major concern. But imagine processing millions of records or reading a very large file.

Generators can be useful because we do not always need to store every result at the same time.

The important idea for now is that return usually finishes a function, while yield produces a value and allows the function to continue later.

slides.title: Inspect a generator with next()
slides.transcript:
This slide helps us see more clearly how a generator works.

We have a countdown function.

The function starts with n, and as long as n is greater than zero, it yields the current value and then decreases n by one.

Notice that when we write g equals countdown three, Python does not immediately run the entire countdown.

Instead, g becomes a generator object.

Then we call next g.

The first call starts the function and gives us three.

The generator pauses at the yield statement.

When we call next again, the function continues from that exact location. It decreases n and eventually yields two.

This is one of the most important things to understand about generators.

They maintain their state between requests.

Run the example and look at the two values.

Then, if you want to experiment, add another print next g.

You should get one.

If you call next one more time after the generator is finished, Python will raise StopIteration. That simply means that the generator has no more values to produce.

slides.title: Debugging Techniques
slides.transcript:
Now let's talk about debugging.

Debugging is not just something we do when our program completely crashes.

Sometimes the code runs successfully but produces the wrong result. Those problems can actually be harder to identify.

One simple debugging technique is to print intermediate values.

Look at the divide function.

Before performing the calculation, we print the values of a and b.

Then, after the division, we print the result.

This gives us a simple trace of what happened inside the function.

Run the example and notice how those debug messages help us follow the execution.

In a real project, you normally would not leave lots of debug print statements everywhere permanently. But while you are trying to understand a problem, they can be extremely useful.

The second example introduces assert.

An assertion lets us tell Python that we expect a particular condition to be true.

Here, we calculate the average of ten, twenty, and thirty.

The average should be twenty.

So we assert that average equals twenty.

If the statement is true, the program continues normally.

Try changing twenty in the assertion to twenty-one and run the code again.

You should see an AssertionError.

Assertions can be helpful while developing and testing code because they make our assumptions explicit.

slides.title: Code Efficiency & Built-ins
slides.transcript:
Let's now think about code efficiency.

When people hear the word optimization, they sometimes immediately think about writing complicated algorithms or trying to make every line faster.

That is usually not the best place to start.

Python already provides many built-in functions that are clear, convenient, and efficient.

For example, imagine that we want the total of a collection of numbers.

We could create a variable called total, loop through every value, and add each number to total.

That works.

But Python already gives us the sum function.

Similarly, max can find the largest value, min can find the smallest value, and len can tell us how many items we have.

In the example, we create a range containing one million numbers and pass it directly to sum.

Run the example and look at the result.

The important lesson is not just that this code is shorter.

It is also easier for another Python programmer to immediately understand what we are trying to do.

Whenever Python already provides a clear built-in operation, it is usually worth considering before writing a manual loop.

slides.title: Measure performance with perf_counter()
slides.transcript:
Sometimes we genuinely need to compare the performance of different approaches.

When that happens, we should measure rather than guess.

Python's time module provides perf_counter.

Perf_counter is useful for measuring elapsed time with fairly high precision.

Look at the example.

First, we create a list of one hundred thousand numbers.

Then we record the starting time.

After that, we calculate the sum.

Finally, we call perf_counter again and subtract the starting time.

The difference tells us approximately how long the operation took.

Run the example.

Your elapsed time may be slightly different every time you run it. That is normal because your computer and browser are doing many other things in the background.

The larger lesson here is about workflow.

First, make sure the code is correct.

Second, make sure it is readable.

Then, if performance actually matters, measure the code.

We should avoid making code harder to understand just because we assume one approach might be faster.

slides.title: Practice: Foundation & Building
slides.transcript:
Now we are moving into practice.

The first example is our foundation exercise.

We want to create a list containing the even numbers from one through ten.

Look carefully at the comprehension.

We loop through the values, and then we use x modulo two equals zero as our condition.

Modulo gives us the remainder after division.

If a number divided by two has a remainder of zero, the number is even.

Before running the cell, try to predict the output.

Then run it and confirm your answer.

After that, try changing the range so it goes to twenty.

The second exercise practices lambda functions.

We create a lambda that accepts two inputs, a and b, and returns their sum.

Then we call the function using three and four.

Run the example.

After you understand it, try changing the lambda from addition to multiplication.

These exercises are intentionally small.

At this stage, I want you to become comfortable reading the syntax before combining too many advanced ideas together.

slides.title: Practice: Intermediate to Mastery
slides.transcript:
This slide contains three practice examples.

Let's start with the generator.

The squares function receives n and yields x squared for each value in the range.

For this small example, we convert the generator to a list so we can easily see all the results.

Remember that the generator itself normally produces the values one at a time.

Next, we have the safe_divide function.

This example is really about defensive programming.

Before dividing, we check whether b is zero.

If it is zero, we return a message instead of allowing Python to perform an invalid division.

Run the example and then change zero to two.

Notice how the behavior changes.

Finally, we compare a manual loop with Python's sum function.

The manual approach starts with total equal to zero and adds each value individually.

Then we calculate the same result using sum.

Both answers should be identical.

This is a useful exercise because it shows that understanding the longer version helps us appreciate what the built-in function is doing for us.

slides.title: Filter adult patient ages
slides.transcript:
Now let's connect list comprehensions to a simple analytical example.

Suppose we have patient ages and we only want records representing adults.

Our original list contains twenty, fifteen, thirty, seventeen, and forty-five.

We define adults as ages greater than or equal to eighteen.

The list comprehension checks every value and keeps only the values that satisfy that condition.

Before running the code, look at the original list and identify which values you expect to remain.

We should keep twenty, thirty, and forty-five.

Now run the example and confirm the result.

This is a very simple dataset, but the analytical idea is important.

Filtering is one of the most common operations in data analysis.

Later, when we use NumPy and Pandas, we will perform similar filtering operations on entire columns and datasets.

The syntax will be different, but the logical question is exactly the same: which observations satisfy the condition that we care about?

slides.title: Mini analytical generator pipeline
slides.transcript:
This slide combines several ideas from the module into one small analytical pipeline.

Let's walk through the function slowly.

The function receives a collection called values.

The first step creates filtered.

We use a list comprehension to keep only numbers greater than zero.

So negative numbers and zero are removed.

The next step creates ranked.

We call sorted and use a lambda as the key.

In this particular example, the lambda simply returns the value itself, so the numbers are sorted from smallest to largest.

Then we loop through the ranked values.

Instead of returning all of them at once, we yield each value individually.

Finally, outside the function, we loop through the generator and print each result.

Before running the example, look at the original values: three, negative one, two, zero, and five.

Negative one and zero should disappear.

The remaining values should be two, three, and five, in sorted order.

Run the cell and verify that prediction.

What I like about this example is that we can clearly identify each stage: receive the data, filter it, sort it, yield the results, and then inspect the output.

That kind of step-by-step structure is very important when analytical workflows become more complicated.

slides.title: Use advanced syntax only when it improves clarity
slides.transcript:
Let's finish Module 7 with the most important message from this lesson.

Advanced Python syntax is useful, but it is not automatically better than basic Python syntax.

A list comprehension is excellent when the transformation or filtering rule is simple.

But if the comprehension becomes very long, a regular loop may be easier to understand.

A lambda works well for a short expression, especially when used as a sorting key.

But if the logic becomes complicated, create a normal named function.

Generators are useful when we want to process values one at a time or avoid storing a large result in memory.

Debugging techniques help us understand what is happening inside our programs.

And built-in functions can often make our code both shorter and clearer.

When thinking about efficiency, remember to measure before optimizing.

The goal throughout this course is not to write code that looks advanced.

The goal is to write code that solves the problem clearly and can still be understood later by you or by someone else.

In the next module, we will build on these ideas and look at more professional Python practices, including exception handling, regular expressions, documentation, Git concepts, style, and testing.
